An interjection is a word, sound, or short phrase that expresses a sudden emotion, reaction, or feeling — things like surprise, pain, joy, disgust, hesitation, or excitement. Think of it as a verbal outburst. It's the kind of thing that jumps out of your mouth before your brain has even finished thinking.

Examples: Ouch! Wow! Hmm. Oh! Ugh. Yay! Hey!
Where It Fits in Grammar

English has eight traditional parts of speech — nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, and interjections. The interjection is the most emotionally raw of them all. While every other part of speech plays a logical, structural role in building sentences, interjections don't build anything. They simply express.
The Most Important Feature: Grammatical Independence

This is the defining quality of an interjection: it has no grammatical connection to the rest of the sentence. It doesn't describe a noun, modify a verb, or link ideas. It just sits there, on its own, doing nothing but expressing a feeling.

Watch what happens when you remove an interjection from a sentence:

"Oh, I forgot my keys."
Remove "Oh" → "I forgot my keys."

The sentence is still perfectly complete. The interjection added emotion, but the grammar didn't rely on it at all. This independence is what separates interjections from every other part of speech.
Where Interjections Appear in a Sentence

Interjections most commonly appear at the beginning of a sentence, but they can also appear in the middle or at the end — or they can stand completely alone.

  • Alone: "Ouch!" (someone just got hurt)
  • Beginning: "Wow, that sunset is beautiful."
  • Middle: "That was, well, not what I expected."
  • End: "You actually did it, huh?"
Punctuation: It Tells You the Intensity

How an interjection is punctuated tells you how strong the emotion is.

  • Exclamation mark (!) → Strong, intense emotion
    "Ouch! That really hurt!"
  • Comma (,) → Mild, gentle emotion
    "Oh, that's a little surprising."
  • Question mark (?) → Doubt, disbelief, or asking for confirmation
    "Really? You're serious?"
  • Period (.) → Flat, deadpan, or understated
    "Hmm." (said when you're thinking quietly to yourself)

The same interjection can carry completely different meanings just by changing the punctuation — and in speech, by changing your tone of voice.
Types of Interjections

1. Primary Interjections (Pure Interjections)

These words have only one job in the English language — to be an interjection. They don't function as any other part of speech. They are often sounds more than real "words."

Oh! Ah! Ouch! Ow! Wow! Phew! Shh! Psst! Hmm! Ugh! Yikes! Whoa! Oops! Ahem! Uh-oh! Yay! Eww!

2. Secondary Interjections (Borrowed Interjections)

These are regular words — nouns, verbs, adjectives — that are borrowed and used as interjections in the right emotional context. Outside that context, they go back to being normal words.

"Shoot!" → normally a verb; used here as an interjection of frustration.
"Man!" → normally a noun; used here as an interjection of disbelief.
"Brilliant!" → normally an adjective; used here as an interjection of approval.
"Nonsense!" → normally a noun; used here as a dismissive reaction.
"Come on!" → normally a verb phrase; used here as frustration or encouragement.
Categories by Emotion

Interjections cover the full range of human emotion. Here is a breakdown of the major emotional categories:

Surprise or shock: Oh! Wow! Whoa! Gosh! Good heavens!

Pain: Ouch! Ow! Yow!

Joy or excitement: Yay! Hurray! Woohoo! Yahoo!

Disgust or repulsion: Ugh! Yuck! Eww! Blech!

Hesitation or thinking: Um... Uh... Er... Hmm...

Relief: Phew! Whew!

Approval or agreement: Yes! Great! Absolutely! Indeed!

Disapproval or disbelief: No! Nah! No way! Seriously?

Calling someone's attention: Hey! Psst! Ahem! Yo!

Realization or understanding: Aha! Oh! I see!

Farewell or greeting: Hi! Hello! Hey! Bye! Goodbye!
How the Same Interjection Can Mean Different Things

The beauty — and complexity — of interjections is that one single word can carry many different meanings, depending entirely on how it is said or written.

Take the word "Oh":

  • "Oh!" → Surprise. Something unexpected just happened.
  • "Oh." → Quiet realization. You just understood something.
  • "Oh..." → Disappointment. Things didn't go the way you hoped.
  • "Oh?" → Curiosity or mild doubt. You want to know more.

Context and tone are everything. The word itself is a blank vessel — the emotion poured into it gives it its meaning.
Formal vs. Informal Usage

Interjections are far more common in spoken language and informal writing — conversations, text messages, fiction, dialogue, and personal writing. In formal academic or professional writing, they are rare and often avoided, because they are inherently emotional and spontaneous, which clashes with the controlled, objective tone that formal writing demands.

In fiction and storytelling, however, interjections are extremely valuable because they make dialogue feel authentic and alive. A character who says "Ugh, I can't believe this" feels far more real than one who says "I am very disappointed by this situation."
A Quick Summary

QuestionAnswer

An interjection is a word, sound, or phrase that expresses emotion or reaction. It is one of the eight parts of speech. Its defining feature is that it stands grammatically independent — it connects to nothing in the sentence and can be removed without breaking the grammar. It gets its meaning almost entirely from tone, context, and punctuation rather than from its literal definition. Interjections can be pure sounds (Ouch, Hmm, Wow) or borrowed everyday words used in an emotional burst (Man! Shoot! Brilliant!). They are the most human, instinctive part of language — the part that arrives before thought does.
